title: Why Palantir Stock (PLTR) Is Still a Buy After Its Q3 Pullback
detail:
Why Palantir Stock (PLTR) Is Still a Buy After Its Q3 Pullback
TipRanks
Thu, November 5, 2026 at 1:32 PM PST 5 min read
PLTR
Trade PLTR on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Palantir Technologies' (PLTR) stock is still a Buy after its Q3 pullback, in my view, because the market may be underestimating the strength of its underlying business. In Q3, the Florida-based software company delivered yet another beat across the board. Revenue reached $2.31 billion, while adjusted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $0.44, beating expectations by 6% and 8.4%, respectively. Still, the stock pulled back after earnings and has fallen about 20% from its October highs.

In my view, the market may be underestimating some key metrics, especially the record net dollar retention (NDR) of 165% and greater visibility into future revenue. While valuation remains the biggest risk, I believe the recent correction has created an attractive opportunity. My projections suggest meaningful upside potential, supporting my Buy rating on PLTR.

The Real Standout from Palantir's Q3

Beyond the headline numbers, one of the most impressive metrics from Palantir's Q3 was NDR, which rose from 157% in Q2 to 165%. Put simply, this means the same customer base generated 65% more revenue over the past 12 months than in the previous 12 months, even after accounting for lower spending or customer losses. Yet what makes this figure truly impressive is the scale at which Palantir is achieving it.

As the chart below shows, Palantir's NDR stood at just 107% in Q3 2023, when the company generated around $558 million in quarterly revenue. Three years later, quarterly revenue surpassed $2.3 billion, while NDR reached 165%. In other words, even after quadrupling its revenue, Palantir managed to sharply accelerate spending growth among its existing customers.

To put this into perspective, Snowflake (SNOW), another major software and data company, reported an NDR of 126% in its most recent quarter. Although the two companies calculate NDR somewhat differently, this comparison helps show just how impressive Palantir's result is.

Palantir's Growth Story Has More Visibility than Ever

Perhaps the biggest benefit of such a high NDR is greater visibility into future revenue growth — something investors highly value. Unlike companies that must constantly win new contracts to grow, Palantir already has an established customer base that keeps increasing its spending.

NVDA

Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and Palantir (NASDAQ: PLTR) are two of the hottest AI stocks around. Each company is posting strong growth, but I think only one is a buy right now.

By 2027, these two companies will have dramatically different valuations, and that will be the deciding factor between the two.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Nvidia and Palantir are two different styles of AI investments

Nvidia and Palantir operate in two entirely different sectors of AI.

Nvidia is on the infrastructure side, as it makes graphics processing units (GPUs) and various products to support them. GPUs are powerful parallel processors that excel in applications that require maximum computing power. They also can be configured to handle a wide array of computationally heavy workloads. Nvidia's GPUs are the best available, and they have won a majority of the data center AI accelerator market as a result.

While a lot of AI infrastructure has been built, much more remains to come. Nvidia estimates that the big five hyperscalers will spend nearly $800 billion on capital expenditures this year. For next year, it estimates that figure will rise to $1.3 trillion.

That's strong growth, and Nvidia has already revealed its own estimated 2027 revenue growth rate: 70%. That's an impressive figure for a company of Nvidia's size and makes it a solid investment.

Palantir is on the application side of AI. Its AI-powered data analytics software is becoming widely used by both governments and commercial clients. While Palantir got its start in the government space, its U.S. commercial revenue surpassed its government revenue for the first time in Q3.

In Q3, its revenue rose 96% year over year. That continued a long trend of accelerating revenue growth.

Additionally, Palantir isn't a growth-at-all-costs company that's putting profits second. It posted a net income margin of 49%, showcasing its strong profitability.

Accurately predicting next year's growth isn't as easy with Palantir. Analysts have consistently underprojected its top line, and with their consensus forecast for revenue to grow only 51% next year, that could be happening again. However, those consensus figures are still the best projections investors have to work with.

Nvidia has no 2027 growth priced in

When it comes to weighing companies' valuations, I think measuring their stock prices relative to analysts' earnings estimates for their next year is the best approach. However, we'll need to tweak how we gauge Palantir due to the analyst community's poor track record on predicting its results.

Red Cat (RCAT) fell 45% and AeroVironment (AVAV) 26%, placing Ondas in the middle of a speculative, high-beta group retreat.

Bulls cite $1.4 billion in cash and a $757 million backlog; bears counter with heavy losses and shares ballooning from 80 million to 504 million.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

A sector-wide retreat from high-beta drone and defense-tech stocks has caught Ondas (NASDAQ:ONDS), even as the company's revenue keeps growing. Ondas stock is down 38% over the past month to $4.58. That slide leaves the stock down 53% year to date (YTD), a sharp reversal for a company that has spent the year buying its way into counter-drone, loitering munition and defense robotics markets.

Thinkstock

The question for shareholders is whether the decline reflects broken fundamentals or a volatile stock getting swept up with its group. Ondas stock carries a beta of 3.082, so it tends to swing far harder than the broad market in both directions.

How a Drone Stock Sell-Off Dragged Ondas Lower

High-beta drone and defense-tech stocks have sold off hard in recent weeks, and a risk-off move in speculative growth stocks after the midterm elections added pressure this week. Ondas has moved with that tide, and its closest peers tell the same story.

AeroVironment (NASDAQ:AVAV) stock is down 26% over the past month to $102.55, a milder decline than Ondas has posted. Red Cat Holdings (NASDAQ:RCAT) stock is down 45% over the past month to $3.46, a steeper drop than Ondas. Taken together, the two peers place Ondas in the middle of a sector-wide sell-off, with one rival falling less and one falling more.

------

How Ondas Differs From AeroVironment and Red Cat

Ondas has built its business through acquisitions, putting together a system-of-systems portfolio that covers counter-drone defense, loitering munitions, stratospheric surveillance and unmanned ground vehicles. SkyWeaver, an edge-AI platform Ondas is developing with Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR), is designed to tie those systems into customers' command-and-control networks.

By contrast, AeroVironment is an established defense contractor. Its lineup runs from Puma reconnaissance drones and Switchblade loitering munitions to directed-energy and cyber systems, sold largely to the U.S. Department of Defense. Red Cat is a smaller drone maker built around its Black Widow small unmanned aircraft, with a newer push into uncrewed surface vessels, while integration matters more for Ondas than for either peer since its growth depends on integrating many recently acquired businesses together.

Bull Case for Ondas: Cash, Backlog and a Steep Revenue Ramp

Ondas, then named Ondas Holdings, announced on January 12 that it had closed a $1 billion stock and warrant offering. The company said the shares and warrants priced above market. At the end of June, Ondas held $1.4 billion. The holdings were in cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash and short-term investments, which could give it room to fund its drone and defense expansion without near-term cash pressure. Management noted the company kept significant financial flexibility even after deploying $325 million in Q3 2026 to close the DZYNE and Cyberhawk acquisitions.

The bulls also point to the August 13 report, when Ondas posted Q2 2026 revenue of $83.8 million, up 67% from the prior quarter and more than 13x the year-earlier level. Along with those results came a higher full-year 2026 revenue target of $525 million to $550 million and a pro forma backlog of $757 million. Demand for drones and counter-drone systems from militaries and governments offers a long-term boost for that portfolio. Sell-side ratings lean bullish as well, with three Strong Buy ratings, seven Buy ratings and no Hold or Sell ratings.

ONDS Earnings Explorer — 24/7 Wall St.
Bear Case for Ondas: Losses, Dilution and Sector Momentum

Profitability is still a long way off for Ondas. The company's Q2 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) loss was $51 million, and its earnings per share (EPS) of -$0.14 missed expectations of -$0.09. Company-wide adjusted EBITDA profitability isn't expected until Q4 2027, according to management.

Dilution is the second worry. Ondas's January raise issued a large block of new shares and warrants, and its share count climbed from 80,178,416 at the end of 2024 to 503,593,000 at the end of June.

Sector momentum cuts against Ondas too, since the stock trades with a speculative group that can keep falling, and uncertainty in Washington over defense budgets after the midterms adds another layer of risk. Management has highlighted supply-chain challenges and possible second-half gross margin pressure from product mix.

What Comes Next for Ondas After Its Steep Monthly Slide

The next test for Ondas is its upcoming Q3 results. The results should show the second-half delivery ramp management has promised, including volume shipments against more than $240 million of orders under the U.S. Army's $982 million lethal unmanned strike program. Beyond earnings, watch for new contract announcements and signs that cash burn is slowing as revenue scales.

To the bulls, Ondas is a well-funded company with a fast-growing backlog caught in a sector-wide sell-off. The skeptics might counter that the company is still burning cash, adding shares and trading at the mercy of a momentum-driven group. A conservative investment approach could make sense until the issue of Ondas's delivery ramp resolves.

Key Takeaways

Palantir shares fell 10% today as the post-midterm sell-off in AI and defense stocks deepened, with no news from the company.

U.S. government customers brought in 41% of Palantir's third-quarter revenue, so a tighter Pentagon budget reaches the smaller part of its sales.

Lockheed Martin fell far less today than Snowflake, pointing to AI valuations as the bigger force behind the drop.

Palantir's first 2027 guidance, due in early February, is the next real test.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR:NASDAQ) is down 10% today, with no news of its own, as the post-election sell-off in AI and defense stocks rolled into a second day.

Defense stocks took the first hit on Wednesday, when Lockheed Martin (LMT:NYSE) fell about 7% after Democrats won both chambers of Congress. Today, Lockheed is down just 2%, and the selling has moved to AI names like Snowflake (SNOW:NYSE), down 6%.

Uncle Sam is the smaller customer now

Congress sets the Pentagon's budget, and President Trump asked for $1.5 trillion for 2027, against the $901 billion approved now. Jefferies expects something closer to the House's plan of about $1.15 trillion. Even that would be roughly 28% more than the current budget.

And Washington matters less to Palantir than it used to: in the third quarter, U.S. commercial revenue passed U.S. government revenue for the first time. U.S. government customers brought in $953 million of the quarter's $2.31 billion, its 10-Q shows, up 96%.

Analysts expect revenue to quadruple from 2025 to 2028:

Nothing in today's news should change this year's number, and at today's mix, most of the $12.4 billion expected for 2027 would come from customers outside Washington.

Priced like an AI stock

AI infrastructure is taking the bigger hit. Bloom Energy (BE:NYSE) is down 17% today, even after NTT DATA announced a 900 MW fuel cell agreement with Bloom at 9 a.m. ET.

Lockheed, with a record $292 billion backlog, trades at 20x forward earnings and held up better today. Snowflake, whose product revenue grew 37% in its July quarter, trades at 115x and fell. It reports on Dec. 2.

Palantir's forward P/E, 94x before today, has swung widely over five years:

That's below its five-year average of 102x and far from its 270x peak in October 2025, and today's drop takes it lower still.

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR) turned in another quarter of impressive results, as revenue growth once again accelerated. However, the stock dipped on the news and is down more than 15% over the past year.

Let's dig into Palantir's Q3 results and prospects to see why I think it could become one of the biggest winning artificial intelligence (AI) winners of the next decade.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Another great quarter

For the 13th straight quarter, Palantir's quarterly revenue growth accelerated. Its year-over-year revenue growth has now gone from 13% in Q2 2023 to 96% in Q3 2026.

Its Q3 revenue of $2.31 billion also handily topped management's prior forecast of $2.16 billion to $2.164 billion and the analyst consensus of $2.18 billion, as compiled by LSEG. Adjusted earnings per share, meanwhile, surged from $0.18 to $0.44, besting the $0.41 consensus.

U.S. commercial revenue yet again led the way, as customers continue to embrace and expand their use of its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP). U.S. commercial revenue surged 148% to $984 million in the quarter, while U.S. commercial remaining deal value climbed 79% to $6.52 billion. Meanwhile, the company closed U.S. commercial deals worth $1.46 billion in total contract value in the quarter, an 11% year-over-year increase.

In my view, the most impressive metric from Palantir's report was once again its net revenue retention, which measures revenue growth from existing customers that have been with the company for more than a year. This expanded to 165% from 157% in Q2, showing how quickly existing customers are increasing their spending with Palantir. This metric also shows how valuable its customers believe its platform is.

Palantir also continues to add new customers, with its U.S. commercial customer count climbing by 29% year over year and 5% sequentially. Its overall customer count increased by 20% year over year and 4% sequentially.

On the government side of its business, revenue surged 81% year over year to $1.15 billion. U.S. government revenue skyrocketed 96% to $953 million. International government revenue, meanwhile, increased by 31% to $192 million. Its smaller international commercial segment revenue rose by 21% to $184 million.
